prompt: Under The Hound of the Baskervilles, a detective story, the nearest book was Wuthering Heights, a romance. Why?
hint: Read the two blurbs side by side.

choices.text: The model read the genre field and both books are gothic
choices.why: The genre field was not embedded, and it says mystery for one and romance for the other.

choices.text: Both books were written by members of the Brontë family
choices.why: The Hound is by Arthur Conan Doyle; and the author's name was not in the embedded text anyway.

choices.text: Both blurbs are set on the moors and turn on a family
choices.why: Right. The vectors were made from title and blurb, and those two blurbs describe similar places and situations.

choices.text: At scores around 0.4 the order is random from one run to the next
choices.why: The model has no randomness: the same text gives the same vector, and the same order, every run.

prompt: A catalogue has 40 books, 8 in each of 5 genres. If each book's 5 nearest neighbours were picked at random among the other 39, how many of the 200 neighbours would share the book's genre, on average? Give one decimal.
hint: For one book, 7 of the 39 others share its genre. `genres.py` did the same sum for 60 books.

prompt: Writing the genre in front of each title and blurb raised the same-genre neighbours from 94 to 235 of 300. What does that show?
hint: Did the model change, or did its input?

choices.text: The model got better at understanding blurbs
choices.why: The model is identical in both runs; only the text it was given changed.

choices.text: What you embed decides what counts as similar
choices.why: Right. The same model, given the genre as its first words, now places books by shelf; the choice of text is a design decision.

choices.text: The genre labels in the data were wrong before
choices.why: The labels were the same in both counts; they were simply not part of the text the first time.

choices.text: The title-and-blurb vectors had not been normalised
choices.why: Every vector all-MiniLM-L6-v2 returns has length 1, in both runs.

prompt: Recommending books from what they are, their title and blurb, rather than from who bought them, is called ___-based recommendation.
hint: It reads what is inside the book's record.

prompt: Marginalia starts embedding each book as its author's name, its title and its blurb. What happens to the row under a Verne novel?
hint: Think about what two Verne books now have in common as text.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the model skips proper names
choices.why: The model embeds every word it is given; Bleak House was found for a query by one word of its title.

choices.text: Only books by Verne can appear in the row from then on
choices.why: Shared text raises a score, it does not exclude anything; other books still compete on everything else in their blurbs.

choices.text: Every score falls, because longer texts give shorter vectors
choices.why: Every vector from this model has length 1, however long the text.

choices.text: Verne's other books move up, now sharing his name
choices.why: Right. Shared words pull vectors together, as the genre did; the row now leans towards the same author, which the author cap was there to limit.

prompt: How does `reader.py` build a vector for a reader?
hint: It uses nothing but the books she finished.

choices.text: The average of her finished books' vectors, renormalised
choices.why: Right. Then her recommendations are the unread books nearest that direction.

choices.text: The vector of the most recent book she finished
choices.why: Every finished book counts, and equally; the program does not know the order she read them in.

choices.text: A vector learned from what the other readers finished
choices.why: That is collaborative filtering, which this lesson describes and does not build.

choices.text: The embedding of her name and her account details
choices.why: Nothing about the reader herself is embedded; only the books' titles and blurbs are.

prompt: Lia's two books have a similarity of 0.207, and their average had length 0.777. Another reader has finished two books whose similarity is 0.6. What is the length of her average, to three decimals?
hint: The squared length of a + b is 2 + 2 × (a · b) for unit vectors; then halve the length.

prompt: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes scores 0.411 against the Hound, nearly as high as Wuthering Heights, yet it is not on Lia's list. Why not?
hint: Her vector is built from two books.

choices.text: Lia has already finished it
choices.why: She finished Pride and Prejudice and the Hound only; the Holmes stories were a candidate like any other.

choices.text: Detective stories are filtered out for readers of romance
choices.why: reader.py applies no rule but skipping finished books; nothing removes a genre.

choices.text: It is far from Pride and Prejudice, and both scores add up
choices.why: Right. The score against the average is the sum of the two, so a book close to only one of hers falls behind books fairly close to both.

choices.text: Recommendations need a score of at least 0.5 against each book
choices.why: There is no threshold: the five highest scores against the average are shown, and Wuthering Heights itself is under 0.5 against both.

prompt: For a reader with unit-length book vectors, what is a candidate's score against her renormalised average equal to?
hint: Write the average as a sum divided by its length.

choices.text: The highest of its scores against any one of her books
choices.why: That would be a different recommender, one that keeps the tastes apart; the average adds the scores instead.

choices.text: Its scores against her books, summed and scaled
choices.why: Right. The constant is the length of the sum of her books' vectors, the same for every candidate, so the ranking is the ranking by the sum.

choices.text: The product of its scores against each of her books
choices.why: A dot product with a sum is a sum of dot products; nothing is multiplied together.

choices.text: Its score against the book she finished most recently
choices.why: The average treats every finished book the same, whenever it was read.

prompt: Order Lia's five recommendations as `reader.py` ranked them, from the highest score to the lowest.
hint: The book between her two tastes came first.
trap: Jane Eyre is last, by 0.001 behind The Scarlet Pimpernel, although it is the other romance on the list.

prompt: Why does `filters.py` walk down the ranking until it has five, instead of taking the top five and removing what breaks a rule?
hint: Count what would survive for Caio.

choices.text: Walking down is faster than sorting the scores
choices.why: The walk runs over a ranking that was already sorted; it saves nothing on sorting.

choices.text: Cutting first would change the books' scores
choices.why: A score depends on two vectors and nothing else; where the list is cut cannot change it.

choices.text: The rules can only be checked against the whole catalogue at once
choices.why: Each rule is checked one book at a time, which is exactly what the loop does.

choices.text: Removing books after the cut leaves fewer than five; for Caio it would leave one
choices.why: Right. His top five held his three finished books and an out-of-stock one, so only one would remain.

prompt: A vector index returns the nearest 50 books for a reader, and the shop's rules then remove 46 of them. How many recommendations does the reader get from that one request?
hint: Rules applied after the search can only remove.

prompt: Why is "one book per author" applied as a rule on the data rather than left to the similarity of the vectors?
hint: What text went into each vector?

choices.text: That field never went into the embedded text
choices.why: Right. The vectors were made from title and blurb; sameness that lives in a field the model never read has to be checked against that field.

choices.text: Embeddings cannot represent people's names
choices.why: They can represent any text they are given; the name was simply not part of this text.

choices.text: Comparing authors through vectors is forbidden by the catalogue's licence
choices.why: No licence is involved; the reason is what the vectors were built from.

choices.text: MMR already removes a second book by the same author
choices.why: It did not: Around the World in Eighty Days stayed beside another Verne at every λ.

prompt: Match each measure in this lesson to the problem it prevents.
hint: Two are rules on the books' data; one works on the vectors.

pairs.right: Recommending a book the reader already has
Offering what the shop cannot sell
Two authors holding four of five places
Five suggestions that resemble each other

right_distractors: A new reader with no history

prompt: What list does MMR give with λ = 1?
hint: Look at what the second term is multiplied by.

choices.text: The books in a random order
choices.why: Nothing in MMR is random; at λ = 1 it is the ordinary ranking.

choices.text: The most varied list it can make
choices.why: Variety only counts as λ falls; at 1 it does not count at all.

choices.text: The plain similarity ranking
choices.why: Right. 1 − λ is 0, so resemblance to the picks costs nothing; mmr.py's first list matched reader.py's.

choices.text: The books sorted by author
choices.why: MMR never reads the author; it compares vectors.

prompt: At λ = 0.5, Persuasion, a romance scoring 0.176 against Caio, took second place. Why?
hint: Half the value is relevance, half is difference.

choices.text: It is Caio's closest unread book
choices.why: It is the furthest from him of anything on the four lists; Journey to the Centre of the Earth, at 0.536, is the closest.

choices.text: It resembles nothing already picked, and at 0.5 being different counts as much as being relevant
choices.why: Right. MMR did what the setting asked; the setting was too low for this catalogue.

choices.text: MMR always adds one book of each genre
choices.why: MMR knows nothing of genres; it compares vectors, and at λ = 0.7 the list had no romance at all.

choices.text: λ = 0.5 removes every science-fiction book after the first
choices.why: Around the World in Eighty Days and Moby-Dick are adventures, and nothing removes a genre; the penalty is about resemblance to the picks.

prompt: With λ = 0.7, a book has a similarity of 0.40 to the reader, and its highest similarity to a book already picked is 0.50. What is its MMR value?
hint: λ times the first, minus (1 − λ) times the second.

prompt: Choosing results one at a time, each paying a penalty for resembling those already chosen, is called maximal marginal ___.
hint: The R in MMR.

prompt: The Lost World was ready to recommend before a single copy was sold. What made that possible?
hint: Where does a book's vector come from in this lesson?

choices.text: It copied the vector of the most similar book in the catalogue
choices.why: It got its own vector from its own text; Journey to the Centre of the Earth was only its nearest neighbour.

choices.text: Three readers had to finish it first
choices.why: Nobody had read it; that is the point of the example.

choices.text: New books are shown first to every reader
choices.why: Only Caio and Íris would have seen it in their top five; the rest would not.

choices.text: Its vector comes from its own title and blurb
choices.why: Right. Content-based recommendation needs nothing from readers, so a new book is placed on its first day.

prompt: Marcos has an account and has finished nothing. Why can `reader.py` not produce a list for him?
hint: What is his vector made from?

choices.text: The average of no vectors is not a vector
choices.why: Right. With nothing finished there is nothing to average, so the fallbacks are popularity or asking him.

choices.text: His account is too new for the model to accept
choices.why: The model never sees accounts; it only embeds text.

choices.text: The model refuses readers who have no name on file
choices.why: Marcos has a name; and the model never sees a reader's name either.

choices.text: His vector would be all ones and match every book equally
choices.why: There is no vector at all to be all ones; the mean of an empty list is undefined.

prompt: A large shop with millions of readers adds a new book this morning. Which approach can recommend it today?
hint: What does each approach need to have a vector for the book?

choices.text: Collaborative filtering, because millions of readers are plenty of data
choices.why: The data is about other books; for this one there is no reader at all, so it has no vector there.

choices.text: Both, since both end up comparing vectors
choices.why: They compare vectors once they have them; only one of them can make a vector for an unread book.

choices.text: Content-based, because it embeds the blurb
choices.why: Right. Collaborative filtering learns a book's vector from who read it, and nobody has; millions of readers of other books do not help this one.

choices.text: Neither, until the book has sold at least one copy
choices.why: The Lost World was placed from its blurb alone, before any sale.

prompt: Asked for "ghost stories and haunted houses", the search found The Turn of the Screw first and Bleak House, a novel about a lawsuit, second. Why Bleak House?
hint: Look at its title.

choices.text: Bleak House is a ghost story in the catalogue
choices.why: Its blurb is about an inheritance lawsuit in London's courts; its genre is literary.

choices.text: Dickens is the most popular author among the readers
choices.why: Popularity is not part of the score; the search only compares the query's vector with the books'.

choices.text: The query was embedded with a different model from the books
choices.why: coldstart.py embeds the query with the same embed function as the books; otherwise none of the scores would mean anything.

choices.text: Its title has *house*, which weighs a lot in a short query
choices.why: Right. The title is part of the embedded text, and in a five-word query one shared word moves the score a long way.

prompt: Put in order what `filters.py` does to give Caio five recommendations, starting from nothing.
hint: The books are embedded before anything is known about Caio.
items: Embed every book's title and blurb
Average the vectors of the books Caio finished and renormalise
Score every book against that vector and sort
Walk down the ranking, skipping books that break a rule
Stop when five books have been picked
trap: The rules are applied during the walk, not before the ranking and not after a cut at five.

prompt: Nina has finished one book, Around the World in Eighty Days. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: An average of one.

choices.text: Her vector is that book's vector
choices.why: Yes. The average of one unit vector is the vector itself.

choices.text: Her list is the row under that book
choices.why: Yes. reader.py r12 and like.py b28 printed the same five books with the same scores.

choices.text: Her average had length 1.000 before renormalising
choices.why: Yes. One vector of length 1 averages to itself, so there was nothing to renormalise.

choices.text: Her list can only contain adventure books, the genre she read
choices.why: Her list had four science-fiction books and a mystery; genre is not a rule here.

choices.text: She needs the popularity fallback, like Marcos
choices.why: One book is enough to build a vector; the fallback is for a reader with none.

prompt: Match each reader or book to how this lesson's recommender handles it.
hint: One of them has no vector at all.

pairs.right: Embed its blurb; it can be recommended at once

pairs.left: a reader who has finished nothing
pairs.right: Show what is popular, or ask what they like

pairs.left: a reader with one finished book
a reader with two different tastes
pairs.right: A list from the point between them
